title: Correlated Insulator Moiré Bolometer
authors: L. Elesin, A. L. Shilov, M. Kravtsov, X. Zhou, M. Lukianov, A. Kuksov, S. Jana, I. Iorsh, R. Izmaylov, K. Shein, I. Gayduchenko, T. Taniguchi, K. Watanabe, K. S. Novoselov, G. N. Goltsman, A. Principi, D. A. Bandurin
abstract: Light incident on an insulator is generally not expected to turn it into a metal without invoking intense ultrafast excitation that leads to transient structural transitions. Here we show that magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene tuned to half filling of the moiré band provides a notable exception to this expectation. We find that weak beam of long-wavelength photons, with energies comparable to the flat-band width, selectively heat the low-heat-capacity electronic subsystem, thereby suppressing the correlated gap. This produces a giant resistance change governed not by a persistent photocarrier population, but by the extreme sensitivity of a many-body correlated gap to weak electronic heating. The resulting photon-driven insulator-to-metal transition produces a broadband low-noise photoresponse with voltage responsivity exceeding millivolts per nW of absorbed power. The mechanism is dual to superconducting hot-electron response: radiation-heated electrons suppress a many-body order, but in reverse the correlated insulator melts into a metal, providing robustness to magnetic fields of several tesla and a sharp insulator-to-metal resistive contrast. Our results establish correlated flat-band systems as a platform for ultra-sensitive detection of faint long-wavelength radiation.
summary: The authors demonstrate that weak far-infrared light can induce a giant insulator-to-metal transition in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene by selectively heating the electronic subsystem. This effect stems from the extreme sensitivity of the correlated many-body gap to thermal excitation, establishing MATBG as an ultra-sensitive bolometric detector for faint long-wavelength radiation.
main_problem: To investigate if weak, low-energy photons can destabilize a correlated insulator (CI) state in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) and drive it metallic, producing a giant photoresistive response.
main_result: The CI gap collapses upon irradiation due to electronic heating, leading to a broadband, low-noise photoresponse with high voltage responsivity. This mechanism is robust against magnetic fields and does not require structural transitions.
method: Measurements involve mapping the longitudinal resistance ($R_{xx}$) under varying magnetic fields and temperature while irradiating the MATBG device with far-infrared (FIR) or millimeter-wave (MM) photons.
model_or_system:
The physical system is Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) tuned to half filling of the moiré band, which exhibits correlated insulating states at integer fillings ($
u=\pm 2$). The physics relies on the extreme sensitivity of a many-body correlated gap to weak electronic heating.
key_observables: Photoresistance ($R_{	ext{THz}}$), voltage responsivity (exceeding millivolts per nW), and the collapse of the correlated insulating gap ($\omega_g 	o 0$).

Filling factor ($
u$), magnetic field ($B$) up to several tesla, incident photon energy comparable to the flat-band width, and electronic temperature rise ($\Delta T_e$).
main_assumptions: The photoresponse is governed purely by electronic heating suppressing the many-body gap, rather than persistent photocarrier population or lattice dynamics.
figures_summary:
Figures show $R_{xx}$ dependence on filling and magnetic field, demonstrating CI states. Other figures map broadband photoresistance ($R_{	ext{THz}}$) vs. $
u$ and $B$, confirming the electronic origin of the response.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the CI state in MATBG, demonstrates that weak FIR/MM irradiation causes a giant resistance drop by heating the electron subsystem (CI gap collapse), quantifies this photoresponse's high sensitivity, and contrasts this mechanism with superconducting bolometers while analyzing thermalization processes.
why_interesting: This work provides an experimental platform demonstrating how subtle changes in electronic temperature can trigger macroscopic phase transitions (insulator-to-metal) in strongly correlated systems using low-energy photons, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum criticality and energy detection.
